gaps.sentence: Nobody explained the reason ___ the flight was cancelled.
gaps.explanation: 'Why' introduces the cause after 'the reason'; it means 'for which'.

gaps.sentence: Anyone ___ wants to join the trip should sign up today.
gaps.explanation: 'Anyone who' is the standard pattern; 'who' is the subject pronoun for people.

gaps.sentence: This is the worst storm ___ we have had for years.
gaps.hint: after a superlative ('the worst'), use this pronoun
gaps.explanation: 'That' follows superlatives in defining relative clauses; 'which' is considered poor style there.

gaps.sentence: The new bridge, ___ cost two billion euros, opened last month.
gaps.hint: thing + extra information after a comma
gaps.explanation: 'Which' introduces non-defining clauses about things; 'that' is forbidden there.

gaps.sentence: The country is in a situation ___ an election seems inevitable.
gaps.explanation: 'Where' is used with abstract nouns like situation, case and point; 'which' cannot introduce the clause here.

gaps.sentence: The photographer ___ camera was damaged is claiming compensation.
gaps.explanation: 'Whose' shows that the camera belongs to the photographer; 'who's' means 'who is'.

gaps.sentence: The exam, the results of ___ will be published on Friday, was very difficult.
gaps.hint: quantity noun + of + thing in a non-defining clause
gaps.explanation: 'The results of which' joins the clauses formally; 'of whom' is for people and 'of them' cannot link clauses after a comma.

gaps.sentence: The programme ___ I watched last night was about volcanoes.
gaps.explanation: 'Which' refers to things, even when it is the object of the clause.
